title: 'Ex-secretary to PM's graft case: Temporary passport release for Shamsul Iskandar
body: 'KUALA LUMPUR (Oct 5): Datuk Seri Shamsul Iskandar Mohd Akin, a former senior political secretary to the prime minister, has obtained the Sessions Court’s approval for the temporary release of his international passport to enable him to attend several overseas programmes this month. The passport had been surrendered to the court as an additional bail condition after he was charged with five counts of corruption. According to his supporting affidavit obtained by the media, Shamsul Iskandar applied for the permanent return of his passport to facilitate overseas travel in connection with his duties. He said he intends to travel to Frankfurt, Germany, to attend the Frankfurt Book Fair organised by Rex Education from Oct 7 to Nov 11. “Based on my involvement with the Madani Community Leadership Academy, my participation in the book fair aims to foster synergy between organisations and provide mutual benefits to both entities. “Therefore, this participation will provide valuable international exposure to support and strengthen ongoing grassroots initiatives aimed at empowering civil society in line with the Madani principles, particularly through the promotion of literacy, leadership and knowledge,” he said in the affidavit. Shamsul Iskandar also said he had registered to attend the fifth AlBaraka Summit, themed Ethics in Action: Rebuilding Foundations and Advancing the Global Impact of the Islamic Economy, in London scheduled for Oct 13 and 14. He said the summit aims to strengthen ethical foundations for Islamic financial and non-financial institutions, governance systems and market practices. Shamsul Iskandar also said he plans to attend programmes in Ireland, as well as Bosnia and Herzegovina, in November and December. During Monday's proceedings, lawyer Yusmadi Yusoff, representing Shamsul Iskandar, told Sessions Court judge Suzana Hussin that his client had filed an application on Sept 30 for the permanent return of his passport. He also sought its temporary release to enable Shamsul Iskandar to attend programmes in Frankfurt and London this month. Deputy public prosecutor Julaila Jamaludin objected to the application for the permanent return of the passport, saying the supporting documents consisted only of an invitation letter and that the discussions could be conducted online. However, she did not object to the application for its temporary release. Suzana subsequently allowed the temporary release of Shamsul Iskandar’s passport, effective from Monday, on condition that it be returned to the court on or before Oct 16. The court also ordered the prosecution to file an affidavit in reply to the application for the permanent return of the passport by Oct 19, with the decision on the application set for Dec 8. Shamsul Iskandar, 51, faces two charges of agreeing to accept RM140,000 in cash from businessman Tei Jiann Cheing, also known as Albert Tei, as an inducement to assist a company owned by Tei in obtaining approval for a mineral exploration licence in Sabah. He also faces two charges of obtaining furniture and electrical appliances worth RM14,580.03 and RM22,249 respectively, from Tei for the same purpose. The offences were allegedly committed at premises in Jalan Medang Serai, Bukit Bandaraya, and a hotel car park in Jalan Sultan Hishamuddin, as well as at Jalan P14A 1/1, Precinct 14, Putrajaya, between Nov 24, 2023, and March 5, 2024. In a separate charge, Shamsul Iskandar is accused of obtaining gratification amounting to RM64,924 from Tei, allegedly deposited into a CIMB Bank account belonging to Rahmalidya Buyong to cover the rental of a house in Jalan Medang Serai, Bukit Bandaraya, in exchange for assisting Tei's company in securing approval for a mineral exploration licence in Sabah. All five charges were brought under Section 17(a) of the Malaysian Anti-Corruption Commission Act 2009 (Act 694) and are punishable under Section 24(1) of the same Act, which provides for a maximum prison sentence of 20 years and a fine of at least five times the amount or value of the gratification, or RM10,000, whichever is higher, upon conviction. title: 'Brokers Digest: Local Equities - Oil and gas, Sorento Capital Bhd, Bermaz Auto Bhd, UMedic Group Bhd
body: 'Brokers Digest: Local Equities - Oil and gas, Sorento Capital Bhd, Bermaz Auto Bhd, UMedic Group Bhd This article first appeared in Capital, The Edge Malaysia Weekly on September 21, 2026 - September 27, 2026 Oil and gas OVERWEIGHT HONG LEONG INVESTMENT BANK RESEARCH (SEPT 14): Brent has returned above US$100 per barrel as risks rise across Hormuz, Bab el-Mandeb and Saudi’s East-West Pipeline, while Middle East supply disruptions have widened the global oil deficit. China crude imports are also recovering, adding further upside risk to prices. We now expect Brent at US$95-US$100 per barrel towards end-2026 and raise our 2026 assumption to US$90 per barrel from US$80 per barrel. While we retain “buy” calls on most names, we remain selective and favour companies with earnings drivers that can sustain beyond near-term Brent volatility. We advocate positioning for our 2027 thesis of a recovery in Petroliam Nasional Bhd’s (PETRONAS) upstream capital expenditure (capex) alongside rising regional energy-security investments. We believe the sector remains supported by a recovery in offshore support vessel-related names such as Dayang Enterprise Holdings Bhd (KL:DAYANG), Keyfield International Bhd (KL:KEYFIELD) and Perdana Petroleum Bhd (KL:PERDANA), while improving oil and gas services and equipment order flows and longer-term demand for storage, pipelines and broader energy infrastructure should continue to support Dialog Group Bhd (KL:DIALOG) and Wasco Bhd (KL:WASCO). Dialog remains our top pick. We expect Dialog’s earnings to remain well supported in FY27-FY28 by growth across its three key segments. Upstream will be supported by the new Cendramas production sharing contract and Baram Junior Cluster (both commencing from 2QFY27), which are expected to shift the upstream earnings mix higher to 30% to 40%. Meanwhile, Dialog’s downstream earnings visibility remains well supported by several ongoing engineering, procurement, construction and commissioning projects. PETRONAS Chemicals Group Bhd’s (KL:PCHEM) (PetChem) share price has risen around 25% after we upgraded it to “buy” in our end-June report. We are seeing early signs of stabilisation in key product prices, while elevated Brent prices could support further improvement in overall average selling prices in 4QFY26. We expect utilisation rates to improve with minimal turnaround activities at Methanol 2 for 60 days and Fertiliser Sabah for 10 days in 3QFY26, while no scheduled plant turnaround is expected in 4QFY26. PetChem remains attractive, with recovery of urea prices in 2HFY27 as seasonal planting demand returns, and potential divestment of its Pengerang Petrochemical Co Sdn Bhd stake, which could remove significant earnings drag and reduce the group’s foreign exchange (forex) exposure. We view Dayang as a key beneficiary of a potential PETRONAS upstream capex recovery in 2027. Dayang delivered a stronger performance in 2024, when PETRONAS’ upstream spending was relatively elevated at around RM21.5 billion across 2023-2024, while upstream capex remained subdued at only RM9 billion in 1HFY26. Sorento Capital Bhd Target price: 77 sen BUY TA SECURITIES (SEPT 14): Sorento Capital Bhd’s (KL:SORENTO) FY26 gross profit margin reached 45.2%, the highest in the company’s history, despite challenging market conditions arising from the US-Iran war. Management attributes the margin expansion to a reduction in original equipment manufacturing cost in China late last year, which contributed to a stronger 47% gross profit margin in 4QFY26. According to management, global brass prices rose by 50% following the onset of the US-Iran war, leading to higher production cost for bathroom and kitchen taps. However, prices of ceramic bathroom products have been undergoing price cutting. As China’s exports of ceramic products to the Middle East has been disrupted by the war, these products have been redirected to Asian markets, creating downward price pressure. As such, management is confident of sustaining its gross profit margin above 40% for FY27. As far as project sales are concerned, the group has seen an uptick in orders for its Sorento-series sanitary ware. It order book has increased to RM150 million from RM120 million, and we expect the company to secure new orders of RM80 million each in FY27 and FY28. Bermaz Auto Bhd Target price: RM1.35 BUY MAYBANK INVESTMENT BANK RESEARCH (SEPT 14): Bermaz Auto Bhd’s (KL:BAUTO) recovery trajectory continues to outperform market expectations, and we see further upside should the momentum sustain. Near-term margins should improve with stronger support from XPeng China, while Mazda volumes remain resilient. Key considerations include completely built-up (CBU) supply and evolving earnings mix as completely knocked-down (CKD) ramps up. Mazda CBU volume now contributes about two-thirds of sales, which we expect to sustain over the next few quarters until the all-new CX-5 CKD is launched in mid-2027. We expect 5,000 CBU units by year-end, while forex hedging should support CBU margins in FY27. Overall, BAuto’s outlook is underpinned by new Mazda and XPeng model launches, supporting its FY27 sales target of 16,000 units (+23% y-o-y, ex-Kia sales in FY26). Associate earnings are also improving, with Inokom Corp Sdn Bhd returning to profitability and further supported by potential additional assembly contracts. Mazda Malaysia should benefit from CKD expansion, with export volume for the new CX-5 from 2027 (targeting 7,000 units per annum) providing an additional volume boost, while Kia exposure is now minimal. Near-term earnings visibility remains solid, combined with an attractive dividend yield of more than 9%. UMedic Group Bhd Target price: 43 sen BUY MBSB RESEARCH (SEPT 15): The RM47 billion allocated under Budget 2026 and the 13th Malaysia Plan promise of RM40 billion until 2030 continue to support UMedic Group Bhd (KL:UMC). We believe with the upcoming Budget 2027 — which is expected to continue prioritising citizens’ welfare — UMC is positioned for sustained long-term growth by leveraging key industry tailwinds, including hospital overcrowding, medical tourism and an ageing population projected to reach 21% by 2044. To capitalise on these trends, UMC is expected to further expand into ambulatory care by growing its ambulance fleet, scaling its integrated learning and community health centres, and diversifying into the laboratory market and specialised verticals via its Akiteck and Ateria subsidiaries. Additionally, UMC is reinforcing its manufacturing foundation by acquiring three acres of industrial land, expanding clean room capacity and adopting advanced automation to meet rising domestic and global demand across its product portfolio. By incorporating UMC’s FY26 results into our valuation, we revised FY27-FY28 earnings forecasts upwards by 2%. We like UMC for its stable distribution business, paired with its high-margin proprietary manufacturing operations. UMC’s key drivers remain the government’s fiscal support and long-term demographic tailwinds in terms of care demand and medical tourism. Save by subscribing to us for your print and/or digital copy. title: 'Jamin peruntukan awam universiti, hentikan korporatisasi UiTM – Suara Siswa UiTM
body: 'Suara Siswa UiTM menggesa Kementerian Pendidikan Tinggi (KPT) dan Kementerian Kewangan menjamin peruntukan awam yang mencukupi dan berterusan kepada universiti awam, susulan perkembangan terbaharu berkaitan UiTM Holdings yang, menurut kumpulan itu, mencerminkan masalah lebih besar dalam model pembiayaan pendidikan tinggi. Kumpulan mahasiswa itu berkata pengakuan Menteri Pendidikan Tinggi Zambry Kadir pada 27 September bahawa kerajaan tidak lagi menanggung sepenuhnya keperluan kewangan universiti sejak 2017 menunjukkan universiti awam semakin didorong mencari sumber pendapatan sendiri, termasuk melalui syarikat pegangan, pelaburan dan kegiatan komersial. KPT pada masa sama mengakui sebahagian syarikat pegangan universiti tidak berfungsi dengan baik, dan proses meneliti serta menyusun semula syarikat berkenaan telah dimulakan sejak tahun lalu. Menurut Suara Siswa UiTM, UiTM Holdings tidak wajar dilihat semata-mata sebagai sebuah syarikat yang mengalami masalah kewangan. KPT sebelum ini mengesahkan kerugian sebelum cukai terkumpul UiTM Holdings sekitar RM157j bagi 2017, 2018, 2019 dan 2021, manakala Jawatankuasa Kira-Kira Wang Negara (PAC) pernah merekodkan suntikan modal UiTM berjumlah RM260j juta kepada syarikat itu antara 2007 hingga 2018 serta membangkitkan isu pematuhan dan tadbir urus. Kumpulan itu berkata perkembangan berkenaan perlu dibaca bersama dasar kewangan pendidikan tinggi negara. Menurut Pelan Pembangunan Pendidikan Tinggi Malaysia 2015-25 (PPPM) merekodkan sumbangan kerajaan kepada universiti awam bukan universiti penyelidikan turun daripada 85% perbelanjaan operasi pada 2015 kepada 76% pada 2022, sementara pendapatan dijana sendiri meningkat daripada 21% kepada 22%. - Sign up for Aliran's free daily email updates or weekly newsletters or both - Make a one-off donation to Persatuan Aliran Kesedaran Negara (ALIRAN), Maybank a/c 507246118995 or CIMB a/c 8004240948 - Make a regular pledge or periodic auto-donation to Aliran - Become an Aliran member Dokumen itu mengenal pasti kemampanan kewangan sebagai cabaran utama institut pengajian tinggi. Suara Siswa UiTM berkata keadaan itu menunjukkan universiti awam semakin diletakkan di bawah tekanan untuk mencapai kelestarian kewangan melalui penjanaan pendapatan, termasuk pelaburan, kegiatan komersial, konsultansi dan model perniagaan baharu. PPPM secara jelas meletakkan penjanaan pendapatan, pendanaan berasaskan prestasi dan model perniagaan inovatif sebagai sebahagian daripada agenda kelestarian kewangan institusi. [Hala tuju ini diteruskan dan diperkukuh dalam Rancangan Pendidikan Tinggi Malaysia 2026-35.] “Kami melihat persoalan UiTM Holdings sebagai sebahagian daripada masalah korporatisasi pendidikan tinggi,” kata kumpulan itu. “Apabila pembiayaan awam dikurangkan, risiko kewangan tidak hilang, tetapi dipindahkan kepada universiti untuk ditanggung melalui pasaran dan akhirnya kepada mahasiswa melalui pelbagai bentuk kos pendidikan dan sara hidup.” Suara Siswa UiTM menggesa kerajaan mengembalikan pembiayaan awam sebagai asas utama kewangan universiti, dengan peruntukan KPT dan Kementerian Kewangan yang mencukupi untuk menanggung fungsi teras seperti pengajaran, penyelidikan, penyelenggaraan kampus dan kebajikan mahasiswa tanpa memaksa universiti bergantung kepada keuntungan aktiviti komersial. Kumpulan itu turut menyeru supaya yuran dan kos wajib pendidikan dikurangkan secara berperingkat sehingga pendidikan tinggi awam dapat dinyahkomodifikasikan. Kumpulan mahasiswa itu turut menuntut supaya sebarang penyusunan semula UiTM Holdings tidak berakhir dengan sekadar mencari model perniagaan baharu atau menutup kerugian melalui suntikan dana awam tanpa perubahan struktur. Ia mahu kerajaan menilai semula aktiviti komersial universiti berdasarkan kepentingan pendidikan dan masyarakat, di samping memastikan pekerja universiti tidak menjadi pihak yang menanggung kesan penstrukturan. Dalam perkembangan berasingan, Suruhanjaya Pencegah Rasuah Malaysia mengesahkan siasatan terhadap UiTM Holdings masih berjalan dan melibatkan isu teknikal serta kelemahan tadbir urus, termasuk dakwaan pembayaran RM42j berkaitan projek solar 50MW di Gambang, yang dikatakan dibuat tanpa kelulusan lembaga pengarah dan bagi tujuan yang tidak berkaitan dengan projek. Suara Siswa UiTM berkata sebarang pertuduhan jenayah hendaklah tertakluk kepada hasil siasatan dan proses undang-undang, namun isu tadbir urus dan model pembiayaan universiti boleh dipersoalkan secara berasingan. “Universiti awam tidak sepatutnya dipaksa menjadi perusahaan yang mencari keuntungan untuk membiayai fungsi awamnya,” kata kumpulan itu. “Peruntukan pendidikan ialah tanggungjawab negara, manakala kekayaan dan aset universiti harus diprioritikan untuk mahasiswa, pekerja, pengajaran, penyelidikan dan kepentingan masyarakat.” – Suara Siswa UiTM The views expressed in Aliran's media statements and the NGO statements we have endorsed reflect Aliran's official stand. title: 'JBPM sasar pelantikan 24,000 FSM dan FSO, perkukuh keselamatan kebakaran premis - Newswav
body: 'KUALA LUMPUR - Jabatan Bomba dan Penyelamat Malaysia (JBPM) menyasarkan pelantikan 24,000 Pengurus Keselamatan Kebakaran (FSM) dan Pegawai Keselamatan Kebakaran (FSO) menjelang tahun 2030 sebagai langkah perkukuh kawal selia serta aspek keselamatan kebakaran di premis. Ini sekali gus menjadi kompenan penting dalam penubuhan Organisasi Keselamatan Kebakaran (OKK). Ketua Pengarah Bomba, Datuk Seri Nor Hisham Mohammad berkata, bagi pelantikan FSM, jumlahnya dijangka seramai 6,000 orang, manakala pelantikan FSO seramai 18,000 orang. Menurutnya, JBPM melihat sasaran ini sebagai satu keperluan strategik dan setakat ini seramai 498 lantikan telah dibuat membabitkan 174 peserta FSM dan 324 peserta FSO. "Ini merupakan sebahagian daripada keperluan untuk mematuhi Seksyen 27A Akta Perkhidmatan Bomba 1988 (Pindaan 2025) yang mensyaratkan bagi mana-mana premis yang dikenakan penguatkuasaan Perakuan Bomba perlu menubuhkan OKK. "OKK itu perlu ada jumlah yang minimum untuk dilantik dan dalam kalangan itu perlu ada seorang FSM dan tiga orang FSO," katanya dalam sidang akhbar selepas Majlis Pelancaran FSM dan FSO di Menara Merdeka Maybank, di sini pada Selasa. Tambahnya, sebagai persediaan ke arah OKK, JBPM telah melaksanakan pelbagai program libat urus bersama pihak berkepentingan. Katanya, Malaysia mempunyai sekitar 9,451 premis yang ditetapkan dengan profil dan tahap risiko keselamatan kebakaran yang berbeza. "Asasnya ialah bangunan yang telah kita kategorikan di bawah Akta Perkhidmatan Bomba," ujarnya. Jelas beliau, penguatkuasaan OKK secara penuh ini dijadualkan bermula 1 April 2027 sekali gus memberikan tempoh persediaan kepada pihak industri untuk membangunkan kompetensi, struktur organisasi dan tahap pematuhan yang diperlukan. "FSM dan FSO tidak akan mengambil alih peranan JBPM, tetapi melengkapkan ekosistem keselamatan kebakaran melalui pengurusan risiko secara berterusan di peringkat premis," ujarnya. Nor Hisham berkata, salah satu fungsi FSM ialah mengurangkan beban kepada penguatkuasaan berkaitan Perakuan Bomba. "Kalau pada amalan semasa ini berdasarkan prosedur-prosedur semasa kita periksa setiap tahun untuk kita keluarkan Sijil Perakuan Bomba. Tetapi di masa hadapan, tempoh itu akan kita jarakkan lagi. "Laporan pemeriksaan akan disediakan oleh FSM sebelum kita menilai dan membuat pembaharuan," ujarnya. Nor Hisham sebelum itu menyerahkan sijil perakuan kepada kumpulan pertama FSM serta FSO yang memenuhi syarat kelayakan ditetapkan.

title: 'PFI UiTM turut perlu disiasat – KMUiTM
body: 'Kolektif Mahasiswa UiTM (KMUiTM) menggesa Suruhanjaya Pencegahan Rasuah Malaysia (SPRM), Jawatankuasa Kira-Kira Wang Negara (PAC) dan Jabatan Audit Negara menyiasat keseluruhan projek Inisiatif Pembiayaan Swasta (PFI) UiTM, susulan perkembangan terbaharu mengenai tatakelola dan pengurusan kewangan UiTM Holdings. Menurut KMUiTM, perhatian terhadap UiTM Holdings tidak sepatutnya menyebabkan persoalan PFI UiTM yang melibatkan komitmen konsesi jangka panjang dan nilai kewangan yang dianggarkan berbilion ringgit kembali dilupakan, khususnya apabila persoalan mengenai kaedah perolehan dan kos konsesi projek itu telah dibangkitkan sejak 2014. Pada 2014 Rafizi Ramli mempersoalkan enam projek kampus UiTM di Pasir Gudang, Jasin, Seremban 3, Puncak Alam, Tapah dan Kota Samarahan yang menurutnya diberikan melalui rundingan terus, termasuk kepada syarikat-syarikat yang dikaitkan dengan ahli sebuah parti politik. Beliau menganggarkan kos pembinaan enam kampus tersebut sekitar RM1.8bn, berbanding kira-kira RM8.6bn jumlah bayaran konsesi yang didakwanya sepanjang tempoh 23 tahun. Rafizi turut mencabar kerajaan mendedahkan perjanjian konsesi supaya kos, keuntungan pemegang konsesi dan struktur perjanjian dapat diperiksa umum. Pada masa sama, PAC pada ketika itu turut mempersoalkan ketelusan enam projek tersebut dan menggesa maklumat mengenai projek konsesi didedahkan kepada umum, termasuk persoalan penggunaan rundingan terus serta sama ada kerajaan memperoleh value for money. Rekod rasmi Parlimen menunjukkan UiTM menerima RM881j peruntukan pembangunan pada 2022, tetapi RM858j atau 97.3% peratus daripadanya diperuntukkan untuk caj tetap PFI yang merangkumi ‘availability charges, maintenance charges dan maintenance reserve fund’. - Sign up for Aliran's free daily email updates or weekly newsletters or both - Make a one-off donation to Persatuan Aliran Kesedaran Negara (ALIRAN), Maybank a/c 507246118995 or CIMB a/c 8004240948 - Make a regular pledge or periodic auto-donation to Aliran - Become an Aliran member Pada 2023 pula, RM865j atau 95.0% daripada RM911j peruntukan pembangunan diperuntukkan bagi caj tetap PFI. KMUiTM berkata angka tersebut menimbulkan persoalan mengenai kos lepas (opportunity cost) PFI kepada universiti. Setiap ringgit yang diperuntukkan untuk memenuhi komitmen konsesi jangka panjang tidak boleh digunakan pada masa yang sama untuk keperluan pembangunan lain seperti penyelenggaraan kampus, naik taraf fasiliti, pelaksanaan program pembangunan mahasiswa, pengambilan tenaga akademik tetap, pembinaan kolej kediaman serta kebajikan mahasiswa. “Persoalannya bukan sekadar berapa kos sebuah kampus dibina. Persoalannya ialah berapa jumlah yang dibayar sepanjang hayat konsesi dan apa yang UiTM terpaksa korbankan kerana sebahagian besar peruntukan pembangunannya terikat kepada komitmen tersebut,” menurut KMUiTM. Bagi KMUiTM, hakikat bahawa PFI masih mempunyai komitmen kewangan yang aktif menjadikan persoalan lama itu relevan untuk diperiksa semula, bukannya sekadar diarkibkan sebagai kontroversi 2014. Tuntutan itu turut mengambil kira perkembangan terhadap UiTM Holdings. PAC pada 2024 mengenal pasti kelemahan dalam tadbir urus kewangan serta kelemahan maklumat dan kawal selia pengurusan pelaburan UiTM Holdings – manakala SPRM kini menjalankan siasatan terhadap kerugian syarikat berkenaan dan beberapa isu berkaitan, termasuk isu pembayaran RM42j berkaitan projek solar Gambang yang menurut SPRM dibuat bagi tujuan yang tidak berkaitan dengan projek tersebut dan tanpa kelulusan lembaga pengarah. Perbandingan itu, kata KMUiTM, bukan bermaksud mendakwa PFI dan UiTM Holdings melibatkan kesalahan yang sama. Sebaliknya, ia menimbulkan persoalan mengenai standard akauntabiliti terhadap wang awam UiTM. Pada Januari 2026, persoalan tersebut telah pun diketengahkan oleh wakil KMUiTM dalam sidang media mahasiswa mengenai sistem perolehan universiti awam. Mereka ketika itu turut mengangkat semula konsesi kampus UiTM yang dibangkitkan Rafizi pada 2014 dan mengaitkan isu perolehan universiti dengan amanah kewangan awam, selain menggesa audit forensik terhadap projek dan tender universiti. KMUiTM kini menggesa supaya keseluruhan portfolio PFI UiTM dibuka kepada siasatan dan audit, termasuk proses penganugerahan kontrak asal, penggunaan rundingan terus, struktur pemilikan syarikat konsesi, jumlah bayaran yang telah dibuat, baki komitmen, kos penyelenggaraan dan penilaian value for moneyberdasarkan prestasi sebenar projek. Kumpulan itu turut menggesa kerajaan mendedahkan jumlah keseluruhan komitmen PFI yang masih berbaki dan menilai kos lepas kepada fungsi pendidikan UiTM akibat peruntukan pembangunan yang terikat kepada caj PFI. title: 'Santorini Is Calling, And HLB Connect Has Your Ticket
body: '22nd September 2026 - 4 min read Hong Leong Bank is giving HLB Connect users the chance to collect Connect Points through everyday banking activities. The grand prize is a RM20,000 travel voucher for two to Santorini, Greece. The HLB Connect Tap to Escape Promotion 2026 runs from 21 September to 20 November 2026. There are also travel vouchers for Chengdu, a Machines gift card and RM100 cash prizes up for grabs. If you’re an existing HLB Connect user, you can earn points by logging in and completing eligible transactions during the promotion period. You can earn points from things you probably already do, including: You can also earn points from FPX payments, cross-border QR payments, foreign currency conversions and linking an HLB account to an HLB Singapore account via LINKS. Each transaction comes with its own daily and promotion-period limits, so you can’t simply go on a DuitNow spree and expect unlimited points. New HLB Connect users can also earn 500 points by opening an eligible CASA/CASA-i account online and logging into HLB Connect at least once during the promotion period. You can also earn 200 points for each friend or family member who successfully opens an eligible account through the HLB Connect app. The Connect Points aren’t prizes themselves. They’re used to earn entries into the promotion’s prize draws. You’ll need: And your points aren’t deducted when you earn an entry. For example, someone with 11,370 Connect Points would get one entry into the Grand Prize draw, two entries into the Second Prize draw and three entries into the Third Prize draw. You can check your points through the Points Tracker on HLB Connect. Don’t have the app yet? You can download it from the Apple App Store or Google Play Store, then log in and check your points. The grand prize is a RM20,000 travel voucher for two to Santorini, Greece. Two winners will also receive RM10,000 travel vouchers for a trip for two to Chengdu, China. Four winners will get RM5,000 Machines Gift Cards, while another 500 eligible customers will receive RM100 cash prizes based on their accumulated Connect Points after the main prize draws. The promotion is open to new and existing individual customers who use HLB Connect and have an eligible HLB or HLB Islamic current or savings account, HLB Meezani Account-i and/or HLB credit card. However, some previous HLB Connect promotion winners can still participate, but won’t be eligible to win prizes this time around. HLB’s permanent, contract and temporary staff are also excluded from winning. There’s also a one-prize-per-person rule, so you can only win one prize throughout the promotion period. The travel vouchers can be used for flights, hotels, airport transfers and other travel services provided by Holiday Tours & Travel. However, they’re subject to availability, can only be redeemed once, and any costs exceeding the voucher value will have to be paid by the winner. The vouchers are also non-refundable, non-transferable and can’t be exchanged for cash. Winners are responsible for their own travel documents, permits and visas where applicable. For the Machines gift card, it can only be used for physical product purchases at Machines stores in Malaysia, and each gift card can only be used in a single transaction. Any unused balance will be forfeited. The promotion ends on 20 November 2026, with winners due to be notified by 1 February 2027. So, if you’re already using HLB Connect to pay bills, transfer money or make QR payments, you might as well see how many Connect Points you can rack up. Follow us on our official WhatsApp channel for the latest money tips and updates. Christina writes about personal finance with an eye for making the complicated feel straightforward. She is drawn to the everyday money decisions people face and genuinely enjoys finding the clearest way to explain them. Between articles, she is probably napping, on a hiking trail, or terrorising her sister’s cats.

title: 'The socialist tinge running through Malay society and politics | Opinion | The Vibes
body: 'By Murray Hunter A CONSISTENT thread of light, humanitarian socialism, the social-democratic and developmental variety, has long run through Malay society and politics in Malaysia. It appears in traditional cultural traits, interpretations of Islamic social ethics, the policies of major Malay parties including UMNO and PAS, and the structure of the modern economy. This form of socialism today is focused on mutual help, social justice, state intervention for equity, and protection of the community, especially the Malay majority. Private ownership, markets and individual enterprise remain, but they operate within a framework of collective responsibility and guided redistribution, through both the New Economic Policy (NEP) and reserved Malay land. Several deep-rooted Malay cultural traits help explain why such ideas found fertile ground throughout Malaya’s contemporary history. Almost forgotten traditions in the traditional kampong, gotong royong was a practical expression of communal cooperation. Villagers regularly came together to build or repair houses, plant and harvest rice, clear drains and paths, maintain the surau or cemetery, and assist with weddings, funerals and other life-cycle events. The familiar proverb “berat sama dipikul, ringan sama dijinjing” captured the expectation that burdens should be shared. More broadly, Malay society has tended to favour communalism rather than strong individualism. Group harmony, collective responsibility, loyalty to kin and community, and the avoidance of open confrontation often take precedence over assertive personal autonomy or pure self-interest. This cultural orientation creates a natural affinity for policies that stress mutual support, shared welfare and the idea that the community’s well-being is more important than unchecked individual gain. This is partly explained by Malaysia’s high power-distance score on widely used cultural dimensions such as those developed by Geert Hofstede. In high power-distance societies, hierarchy is accepted as normal, and people are generally more willing to follow authority without extensive public questioning. Among many Malays, this has historically translated into relatively high deference to traditional leaders, the state, religious figures and those in positions of formal power. When government programmes are presented as serving the uplift of the Malay community, this readiness to accept direction from above has made large-scale state intervention more readily accepted than it might be in strongly individualistic, low power-distance cultures. The combination of communalism and hierarchical acceptance helped legitimise ambitious top-down social and economic programmes. Islamic teachings have reinforced the same outlook for many. Obligatory zakat functions as a structured redistribution of wealth from those with surplus to the poor, the needy, debtors and other designated categories. The duty to care for orphans, widows and the vulnerable, the prohibition of riba (usury), and the repeated Qur’anic emphasis on adl (justice) have been interpreted by some Muslim thinkers as containing important socialist elements. Early PAS leader Burhanuddin al-Helmy explicitly combined Islamist, nationalist and socialist ideas in the struggle against colonialism and inequality. Malaysian sociologist Syed Hussein Alatas, in his work Islam and Socialism, argued that Islam’s principles of anti-exploitation and social justice made it compatible with non-Marxist forms of socialism focused on fairness and community welfare rather than atheistic materialism or the abolition of private property. In formal politics, the pattern is clear. Early Malay leftist and populist groups drew on ideas of uplifting ordinary people (marhaen). Within UMNO, the decisive shift came after the 1969 racial riots under Tun Abdul Razak. Razak, who had been exposed to British Labour Party and Fabian socialist thought during his studies, spoke of a form of “nationalist socialism” suited to a developing multi-ethnic nation. The New Economic Policy (NEP) that followed introduced large-scale state intervention with two main prongs: the eradication of poverty regardless of race, and the restructuring of society so that Malays and other Bumiputera could participate more fully in the modern economy and no longer be identified primarily with subsistence agriculture. This was deliberate social engineering aimed at equity and national unity. Key institutions created or expanded in the Razak era still shape Malaysia today. FELDA (Federal Land Development Authority) organised large-scale land settlement schemes that moved hundreds of thousands of rural Malay families onto new agricultural plots, complete with housing, infrastructure, technical support and a structured pathway out of poverty. It was a classic state-led redistributive and developmental programme. MARA (Majlis Amanah Rakyat) was established to advance Bumiputera participation in education, skills training, business and entrepreneurship through scholarships, loans, commercial ventures and institutional support. Together with other agencies, these bodies embodied the belief that the state had a positive duty to correct economic imbalances and uplift the Malay community through organised collective effort. There was an assumption that those privileged leaders would always take the interests of the people into action. PAS has contributed its own version of this tinge. Although primarily an Islamist party, it has at various times emphasised welfare provision, rural development, anti-elite rhetoric and social justice framed through Islamic ethics. In the states it has governed for long periods, PAS has pursued policies with clear redistributive and protective elements that appeal to lower-income and rural Malays who value collective support and moral economy over pure market outcomes. That is partly the reason PAS has been in government there for a long period of time. Today’s economy is reflective of this history The contemporary Malaysian economy continues to reflect the Razak-era model and retains strong features of a light socialist or developmentalist system. Government-linked companies (GLCs) play a dominant role in strategic sectors. The public bureaucracy remains large and central in directing economic activity, allocating resources and implementing preferential policies. Equity ownership targets, subsidies, public education and housing programmes, and extensive state involvement in the economy persist. FELDA and MARA continue to operate alongside a wider network of agencies dedicated to Bumiputera economic advancement. Markets and private enterprise function, freehold land ownership is secure, and individual initiative is encouraged, yet they operate within a framework of heavy government guidance and redistributive goals aimed at social and ethnic equity. This is a mixed economy with a pronounced interventionist and welfare character. The Malaysian economy is not laissez-faire capitalism, nor is it Soviet-style central planning. The focus has always been practical and humanitarian, aimed at reducing poverty, correcting historical imbalances, fostering mutual support, and using the state as an instrument of community uplift. Cultural communalism, acceptance of hierarchy, Islamic ethics of justice, and the institutional legacy of Tun Razak’s era have all sustained this approach. The light socialist colouring remains one of the quieter but durable features of Malay society and politics. It can be traced from the kampong practices of gotong royong and communalism, through the cultural readiness to accept authoritative direction for the common good, the ethical teachings of Islam on justice and redistribution, the ambitious nation-building of Tun Razak’s time with institutions such as FELDA and MARA, and the continuing role of GLCs and state guidance in today’s economy. Unfortunately, many politicians today appear to have forgotten this deeper aspect of the Malay political psyche. Too often they have become focused primarily upon their own personal wellbeing, status and material advancement rather than the broader communal and redistributive responsibilities that once animated Malay political culture. When the ethic of shared burden and collective uplift is neglected in favour of private gain, the original spirit that helped shape both society and policy risks being hollowed out. Recovering an awareness of that older communal and humanitarian strand may be necessary if Malay politics is to remain connected to the values that long gave it meaning. – September 4, 2026

title: 'Govt Dividend Receipts Up 1.4% to RM39.55b in 2025 on Higher BNM, Khazanah Payouts — AG’s Report
body: 'KUALA LUMPUR (Oct 5): The federal government received RM39.55 billion in dividends from its investments in 2025, up by 1.4% from RM39.01 billion a year earlier, as higher payouts from Bank Negara Malaysia (BNM) and Khazanah Nasional Bhd outweighed lower receipts from other entities. The dividends came from 20 companies and two statutory bodies, compared with 21 companies and two statutory bodies in 2024. The increase was RM535.06 million compared to last year, according to the latest auditor general’s report released on Monday. Petroliam Nasional Bhd (PETRONAS) paid RM32 billion, unchanged from 2024. BNM paid RM5.25 billion, up from RM2.85 billion, an increase of RM2.4 billion or 84.2%. Khazanah's dividend doubled to RM2 billion from RM1 billion. Bank Simpanan Nasional paid RM25 million, down from RM52 million. Dividends from statutory bodies rose 81.8% to RM5.28 billion, while those from companies fell 5.1% to RM34.27 billion. In all, nine companies and one statutory body paid RM7.43 billion, against RM3.98 billion in 2024, an increase of RM3.45 billion or 86.7%. Twelve companies and one statutory body paid less compared to 2024, as three companies paid the same amount in both years. Piramid Pertama Sdn Bhd, which paid RM2.73 billion in 2024, made no payment in 2025. Dividends from Prokhas Sdn Bhd fell to RM5.6 million from RM56.24 million. Three companies, Perbadanan Nasional Bhd, Malaysia Debt Ventures Bhd and Malaysia Digital Economy Corp Sdn Bhd paid dividends in 2025 after paying none in 2024. Source: TheEdge - 6 Oct 2026

body:

Last week, we dropped by Mid Valley Megamall to check out the Maybank Cash Back Mastercard Platinum showcase. Held at Centre Court from 23 to 27 September, the five-day event had a little bit of everything, from interactive activities to a closer look at the card’s features.

A Station For The Card’s Benefits

The showcase was set up like a stamp-card journey. We picked up a journey card at the start and worked our way through five stations. The first four were More To Discover, Stream For More, More To Enjoy and More To Unwind. Once we had collected all four stamps, we could head to the final stop, Maybank Cafe, and redeem either a ZUS Coffee or a Krispy Kreme doughnut.

The activities at each station were also designed around the card’s benefits. One had a touchscreen game where you had to catch groceries in a basket, a playful take on the card’s 8% cash back on digital lifestyle spending. There were also photo spots with airplane window backdrops featuring destinations like Singapore, Thailand, Japan and South Korea, which are among the countries where the card charges no foreign exchange mark-up fee.

Visitors who applied for the card on-site could unlock three additional activities. These included a Flight Simulator and a Merchandise Redemption station with goodies such as a Maybank tumbler and Lilo & Stitch tote bag. Applicants could also try their luck at a giant Gashapon machine for prizes including a Nintendo Switch 2, Setel vouchers and Grab vouchers.

title: 'Cover Story: Playing the long game at Forest City
body: 'Cover Story: Playing the long game at Forest City This article first appeared in City & Country, The Edge Malaysia Weekly on September 28, 2026 - October 4, 2026 It was a scorching afternoon when Country Garden Pacificview Sdn Bhd (CGPV) executive director and chief of regional industrial business development Kevin Li and regional vice-president Syarul Izam Sarifudin arrived at The Edge’s office in Petaling Jaya, Selangor. The pair had flown in from Johor Bahru to give an update on Forest City, a high-profile project in Johor that has dealt with some hot issues since its inception. “What we achieved [since 2015] up to 2025 was merely concentrating more on our operational stability, resource integration and preparing for our next phase of growth,” says Syarul. “In the early years, we were primarily viewed as a residential real estate developer. But we are now embarking into a new sector — managing townships and driving actual economic nodes of financial and industrial development in southern Johor.” The master developer of Forest City is a joint venture between China-headquartered developer Country Garden Holdings Co Ltd and Esplanade Danga 88 Sdn Bhd. Operating as an independent local management unit under Country Garden Malaysia’s executive umbrella, CGPV is responsible for Forest City’s master plan development and management, industrial park development and Special Financial Zone (SFZ) operation. Officially launched by the Malaysian government with duty-free island status in 2016, the 7,500-acre integrated development covers four reclaimed man-made islands over 5,000 acres and 2,500 acres on the mainland. Located in Iskandar Puteri, it sits along the Straits of Johor near the Malaysia-Singapore Second Link, just 2km across the water from Singapore. The ambitious development has made international headlines over the years, some of them for the wrong reasons, especially since it has fallen short of market expectations in terms of progress, sales and occupancy rates. These challenges were compounded by the Covid-19 pandemic and the well-documented financial restructuring of its parent company amid China’s broader real estate liquidity crisis. “When China’s property market faced a systemic downturn, amplified by global supply chain disruptions, macroeconomic shifts and strict pandemic controls, Country Garden — once China’s top property developer — was caught in the crossfire, just like many other big players in the country. However, late last year, our parent group successfully executed onshore and offshore debt restructurings in China,” says Li, who is also the chief financial officer of Country Garden Malaysia. Regardless of the situation faced by its parent company, he highlights that Country Garden Malaysia operates with complete operational and financial independence. “Since Country Garden entered Malaysia as its first overseas destination back in 2010 and 2011, the local operation has relied on an independent management team. For the past three years, our cash flow has been generated entirely within the country, allowing us to remain self-sustaining in terms of liquidity and debt servicing,” he says, adding that all five of its projects in the Klang Valley and Johor are performing steadily. According to Li, Country Garden Malaysia’s sales and cash collection was RM1.3 billion in 2023, more than RM1.1 billion in 2024, and RM1.3 billion in 2025. “More crucially, we utilised our local cash flows to fully settle bank borrowings and capital market obligations worth about RM2 billion over the past three years, including a RM1 billion sukuk … As at earlier this year, the remaining outstanding amount [of the sukuk] was only RM150 million. We pre-repaid them as our cash flow was comfortable.” With most of its debts cleared, local rating agency RAM upgraded Country Garden Malaysia’s outlook rating from negative to stable in March, reflecting its balance-sheet resilience despite global sector volatility. That financial stability has been supported by developments on the legal front. Malaysian courts have recently upheld the validity of sales and purchase agreements in favour of the developer. Dismissing buyer suits seeking to void contracts for reasons such as media portrayals of the project as a “ghost town”, the courts established that market downturns and post-purchase regret do not constitute grounds for breach. The decisions shield CGPV against speculative contract cancellations and protect its revenue base. “Forest City has completed and delivered 26,000 residential units so far. We understand that we cannot make every single person happy, and it is normal to receive feedback or complaints. We respect the buyers’ legal rights,” Li says. “But we also have our internal KPIs [key performance indicators] to meet. We are pleased to share that customer satisfaction consistently hits above 95% in our surveys and polls. Generally, the majority of our 20,000 residents are happy to live here, or they wouldn’t choose to continue staying. This is evidenced by our growing population.” A city waking up Today, Forest City is home to around 20,000 people living in 66 completed blocks, over 770 acres of the approved 5,000-acre reclaimed island land bank. “If you pass by from Iskandar Puteri towards Batam, you can see the lights on across the residential towers at night,” Syarul says. “It is a night-and-day difference compared with what people experienced immediately after the pandemic in early 2021.” Demographics have shifted significantly, he adds. While buyers were once predominantly mainland Chinese, the current resident base is largely local Malaysians, many of whom commute daily to Singapore or work in nearby industrial parks, as well as expatriates of different nationalities. “The township’s commercial pulse is also quickening,” says Syarul. “The Fisherman’s Wharf commercial street has seen steady footfall, with duty-free shops, eateries and premier banking facilities, including branches of Maybank and CIMB, with Affin Bank and AmBank joining the fold soon.” Forest City attracts between 1.5 million and two million tourists annually. Its crown jewel is Forest City Golf Resort, located on the mainland about 9km from the man-made islands. Featuring two 18-hole international championship courses, it draws golfers from Japan, South Korea and Singapore. There is also an affordable beachfront water park that offers weekend entertainment for visiting families. “Forest City is probably the only sandy beach in Johor Bahru. Otherwise, you have to go to Desaru, which is an hour away. To draw more visitors, we are also collaborating with some watersports academies on courses for adults and children. The beach and water park are very popular during school holidays and weekends, contributing to our growing annual tourist and visitor numbers,” Syarul says. Meanwhile, Network School, a start-up society and experimental community based on Silicon Valley entrepreneur Balaji Srinivasan’s book The Network State, was set up in the township in October 2024. Balaji’s private co-living and co-working hub at Marina Hotel drew hundreds of international digital nomads, crypto enthusiasts and tech workers. However, in July 2026, the Iskandar Puteri City Council (MBIP) revoked the Network School operator’s business licence for breaching local licensing conditions. The management of the school clarified that CGPV operates solely as a commercial landlord, and that the developer is fully cooperating with the local authorities to ensure all commercial tenants adhere to the regulatory framework. Strategic shift Li says while Forest City’s master plan is unchanged, CGPV is shifting its focus towards commercial and industrial developments, in alignment with the government’s broader economic development plan for the state. “We maintain the master plan as it is because, to us, it is still a very fantastic plan even after a decade. Of course, for such a mega development, you have to do it in phases, and there will be small twists and adjustments in between. But overall, we do not have plans to review the master plan. Now, we are embarking on the third phase of development. We foresee the entire master plan being completed only by 2040. It is now 12% to 13% developed,” says Syarul. The biggest “twists and adjustments” to the master plan were its integration into the Johor-Singapore Special Economic Zone (JS-SEZ) and designation as an SFZ. In August 2023, the government announced that Forest City would be designated as an SFZ to boost foreign investment, with incentives such as a 15% income tax rate for skilled workers and lower business operating costs. A year later, the government launched the tax incentive framework for the SFZ, which includes a zero tax rate for single family offices (SFO), a 5% corporate tax rate for fintech and global business services, and concessionary income tax rates. In early 2025, Malaysia and Singapore signed a bilateral agreement to establish the JS-SEZ. Under the agreement, Forest City was formally incorporated as Flagship G, one of nine primary flagship zones within the 3,505 sq km economic zone. “We started [the master plan] with residential and, maybe, this made people misunderstand that Forest City is focusing on high-rise residential developments. The SFZ designation puts us right back on track to [industrial projects],” says Li. “Under the SFZ blueprint, the development is divided into two distinct functional zones, where the island component acts as a core financial services hub, focusing on single-family offices, fintech, foreign payment operating systems and back-office financial services. Meanwhile, the mainland focuses on smart logistics, high-tech manufacturing and global business services.” To encourage direct investments in Forest City, the Malaysian government established the Iskandar Malaysia Facilitation Centre Johor (IMFC-J) at Forest City’s 42-storey primary office tower, Menara Delima Satu, to streamline the investment process. The centre houses 18 government agencies under one roof and acts as a single processing point for foreign investors. “A key cornerstone of the SFZ is attracting family offices. The SC (Securities Commission) set an AUM (assets under management) threshold of RM30 million for family offices setting up in Forest City, a far more accessible entry point compared with Singapore’s S$15 million (RM47.9 million) requirement or Hong Kong’s HK$240 million (RM124.7 million) benchmark,” Li says. Syarul stresses, however, that Malaysia is not competing with Singapore or Hong Kong in the SFO segment but is instead complementing them. “It is about synergy. Under the SFZ rules, family offices in Forest City can invest up to 90% of their AUM globally. This means that investors can set up their operational base here in Forest City at one-third to one-fourth of the operational cost, while still leveraging Singapore’s capital markets just across the strait. It is very attractive to many family offices,” he explains. Under the SFO Incentive Scheme guidelines issued by the SC, it is mandatory to establish a physical office in Forest City to qualify for and maintain SC approval and the accompanying 0% tax incentive. According to Li, over 40 SFOs have secured physical office space in Forest City, with nine having formally received SC approval to date. “We are very positive about this, though we do not have an actual target of having many of them in Forest City in the near future because it is beyond our control and SC has its plan. But it is a strong catalyst in helping to add vibrancy to Forest City because when the offices come, they bring in their professional teams — accountants, lawyers and finance and investment experts,” he adds. Forest City is also targeting global business services. CGPV is in advanced discussions with two major international banking institutions — one looking to relocate its back-office operations from Singapore, and another expanding its operational footprint from Kuala Lumpur. Forest City 2.0 Despite the tailwinds from the SFZ, Li and Syarul acknowledge that transforming the mega project into a self-sustaining regional economy is not without immediate, real-world hurdles. The most pressing challenge currently is cross-border physical connectivity and accessibility. “While the project is geographically proximate to Singapore, seamlessly moving people, goods and daily commuters across borders remains a complex, multi-jurisdictional effort,” says Li. “Furthermore, regional competition from peers like Thailand, Indonesia and Vietnam means that Malaysia must continually sharpen its execution speed and policy delivery to stay ahead.” To close this connectivity gap, Country Garden is taking interim measures while lobbying government authorities for long-term infrastructure approvals. “Before all the major government infrastructure projects are completed, we are bridging the gap ourselves. We currently run daily direct shuttles transferring residents and workers to the Sultan Abu Bakar CIQ Second Link complex,” Li says. For the long term, the developer has submitted plans to the joint Malaysia-Singapore ministerial committee under the Iskandar Regional Development Authority (IRDA) for a dedicated ferry terminal. Once approved, ferry routes will connect Forest City directly to Raffles Marina in Singapore and Batam in Indonesia. “We are also asking the government for assistance to permit a direct highway connection linking straight to Tuas, and to integrate Forest City into upcoming regional rail routes like the RTS [Rapid Transit System], ART [Automated Rapid Transit] and transport corridors heading to Kulai and Senai,” he adds. “Moving people efficiently is crucial to unlocking the full value of the JS-SEZ but because these are country-to-country matters, we have to keep pushing and following up continuously.” Simultaneously, the master developer is pivoting to boosting population density and creating high-value local jobs, away from traditional residential property sales, towards what the team calls “Forest City 2.0”. “We are not launching any more residential projects in the near future, but focusing on clearing the inventory. We will advance commercial and industrial land development earlier than originally scheduled to inject immediate economic vibrancy,” Li says. “Our next focus is to bring in companies and industries to invest or establish their presence here.” Acknowledging the importance of generating sufficient jobs to increase Forest City’s population, CGPV is actively trying to draw data centres, logistics players and manufacturers to its upcoming 418-acre industrial park. “We need to create real economic dynamics. If you don’t generate jobs and economic substance, you cannot sustain a population,” Li stresses. The response to this industrial shift has been positive. In the first half of this year alone, the developer logged over 300 company enquiries and secured a 40-acre industrial land deal with a manufacturer in Phase 1 of the industrial park, paving the way for ready-built factory developments in Phase 2 should market demand sustain. In another strategic partnership, Country Garden recently signed a term sheet with Penang-based Oriental Holdings Bhd (KL:ORIENT) to develop a RM750 million healthcare hub in Forest City, anchored by a 500-bed hospital alongside comprehensive medical supply chain services. “Internationally, we are actively introducing Forest City to big-name [multinational corporations]. It is not so much for their name, but the entire supply chain. We are looking to bring in ‘queen bee’ investors,” Li says. “We have been doing roadshows, especially in China, to introduce the JS-SEZ and Forest City SFZ. We went to Shenzhen and Suzhou, which have some of the most successful industrial parks in China.” Apart from the industrial park, CGPV has also received enquiries from international investors interested in private island parcels. “It is something that we are looking at. Instead of standard residential towers, we can custom-reclaim approved island plots, such as 1.5 to two acres, based entirely on an investor’s specific operational or residential requirements. It’s about being adaptive to what the current market actually demands,” he says. Road to 2030 and beyond Apart from Forest City, Country Garden Malaysia has four other major developments in Johor and the Klang Valley, executed largely through JVs. “Out of our five projects in Malaysia, four are structured as JVs,” Li explains. “Only Danga Bay is 100% held by Country Garden Malaysia. We welcome JVs because local partners bring value to the table, though for master site design, we prefer to lead.” In Johor Bahru, Country Garden Central Park has completed three phases comprising over 3,000 residential units that are nearly fully sold. The developer is now planning subsequent sub-phases over a 10- to 12-year development cycle. In Kuala Lumpur, the initial two phases of township development Lake City in Taman Wahyu are completed and sold out, with Phase 3 scheduled for launch next year. The remaining four parcels have been earmarked for development over a 15-year period. In Semenyih, Selangor, residential development Diamond City launched its final landed parcel in September 2025, which is expected to wrap up construction within two years. With a substantial land bank in its existing portfolio, the developer will focus its resources on executing its active pipeline over the next decade. As the interview draws to a close, both Li and Syarul reflect on the long-term nature of master township development. “Rome was not built in a day,” Li says. “When we first came to this coastal area in Johor, it was completely rural. Today, the infrastructure is firmly established. Development never moves in a straight upward line; it moves in spirals, but it always moves forward. “We wish the public to know that since the first day Country Garden has been here in Malaysia, we have wanted to be here long term. Of course, there are twists and turns over the years, but we cannot deny the contribution of the company in Malaysia.” He says Country Garden has invested RM32 billion in Malaysia, including RM20 billion in Forest City alone. “We have created jobs, contributed to the country’s tax revenues and trained local skilled workers. Most importantly, after so many challenges and uncertainties, we were here, and we are still here today. The fundamentals are in place, and we have absolute faith in what Forest City will become.” Save by subscribing to us for your print and/or digital copy. This is evidenced by our growing population.” A city waking up Today, Forest City is home to around 20,000 people living in 66 completed blocks, over 770 acres of the approved 5,000-acre reclaimed island land bank. “If you pass by from Iskandar Puteri towards Batam, you can see the lights on across the residential towers at night,” Syarul says. “It is a night-and-day difference compared with what people experienced immediately after the pandemic in early 2021.” Demographics have shifted significantly, he adds. While buyers were once predominantly mainland Chinese, the current resident base is largely local Malaysians, many of whom commute daily to Singapore or work in nearby industrial parks, as well as expatriates of different nationalities. “The township’s commercial pulse is also quickening,” says Syarul. “The Fisherman’s Wharf commercial street has seen steady footfall, with duty-free shops, eateries and premier banking facilities, including branches of Maybank and CIMB, with Affin Bank and AmBank joining the fold soon.” Forest City attracts between 1.5 million and two million tourists annually. Its crown jewel is Forest City Golf Resort, located on the mainland about 9km from the man-made islands. Featuring two 18-hole international championship courses, it draws golfers from Japan, South Korea and Singapore. There is also an affordable beachfront water park that offers weekend entertainment for visiting families. “Forest City is probably the only sandy beach in Johor Bahru. Otherwise, you have to go to Desaru, which is an hour away. To draw more visitors, we are also collaborating with some watersports academies on courses for adults and children. The beach and water park are very popular during school holidays and weekends, contributing to our growing annual tourist and visitor numbers,” Syarul says. Meanwhile, Network School, a start-up society and experimental community based on Silicon Valley entrepreneur Balaji Srinivasan’s book The Network State, was set up in the township in October 2024. Balaji’s private co-living and co-working hub at Marina Hotel drew hundreds of international digital nomads, crypto enthusiasts and tech workers. However, in July 2026, the Iskandar Puteri City Council (MBIP) revoked the Network School operator’s business licence for breaching local licensing conditions. The management of the school clarified that CGPV operates solely as a commercial landlord, and that the developer is fully cooperating with the local authorities to ensure all commercial tenants adhere to the regulatory framework. Strategic shift Li says while Forest City’s master plan is unchanged, CGPV is shifting its focus towards commercial and industrial developments, in alignment with the government’s broader economic development plan for the state. “We maintain the master plan as it is because, to us, it is still a very fantastic plan even after a decade. Of course, for such a mega development, you have to do it in phases, and there will be small twists and adjustments in between. But overall, we do not have plans to review the master plan. Now, we are embarking on the third phase of development. We foresee the entire master plan being completed only by 2040. It is now 12% to 13% developed,” says Syarul. The biggest “twists and adjustments” to the master plan were its integration into the Johor-Singapore Special Economic Zone (JS-SEZ) and designation as an SFZ. In August 2023, the government announced that Forest City would be designated as an SFZ to boost foreign investment, with incentives such as a 15% income tax rate for skilled workers and lower business operating costs. A year later, the government launched the tax incentive framework for the SFZ, which includes a zero tax rate for single family offices (SFO), a 5% corporate tax rate for fintech and global business services, and concessionary income tax rates. In early 2025, Malaysia and Singapore signed a bilateral agreement to establish the JS-SEZ. Under the agreement, Forest City was formally incorporated as Flagship G, one of nine primary flagship zones within the 3,505 sq km economic zone. “We started [the master plan] with residential and, maybe, this made people misunderstand that Forest City is focusing on high-rise residential developments. The SFZ designation puts us right back on track to [industrial projects],” says Li. “Under the SFZ blueprint, the development is divided into two distinct functional zones, where the island component acts as a core financial services hub, focusing on single-family offices, fintech, foreign payment operating systems and back-office financial services. Meanwhile, the mainland focuses on smart logistics, high-tech manufacturing and global business services.” To encourage direct investments in Forest City, the Malaysian government established the Iskandar Malaysia Facilitation Centre Johor (IMFC-J) at Forest City’s 42-storey primary office tower, Menara Delima Satu, to streamline the investment process. The centre houses 18 government agencies under one roof and acts as a single processing point for foreign investors. “A key cornerstone of the SFZ is attracting family offices. The SC (Securities Commission) set an AUM (assets under management) threshold of RM30 million for family offices setting up in Forest City, a far more accessible entry point compared with Singapore’s S$15 million (RM47.9 million) requirement or Hong Kong’s HK$240 million (RM124.7 million) benchmark,” Li says. Syarul stresses, however, that Malaysia is not competing with Singapore or Hong Kong in the SFO segment but is instead complementing them. “It is about synergy. Under the SFZ rules, family offices in Forest City can invest up to 90% of their AUM globally. This means that investors can set up their operational base here in Forest City at one-third to one-fourth of the operational cost, while still leveraging Singapore’s capital markets just across the strait. It is very attractive to many family offices,” he explains. Under the SFO Incentive Scheme guidelines issued by the SC, it is mandatory to establish a physical office in Forest City to qualify for and maintain SC approval and the accompanying 0% tax incentive. According to Li, over 40 SFOs have secured physical office space in Forest City, with nine having formally received SC approval to date. “We are very positive about this, though we do not have an actual target of having many of them in Forest City in the near future because it is beyond our control and SC has its plan. But it is a strong catalyst in helping to add vibrancy to Forest City because when the offices come, they bring in their professional teams — accountants, lawyers and finance and investment experts,” he adds. Forest City is also targeting global business services. CGPV is in advanced discussions with two major international banking institutions — one looking to relocate its back-office operations from Singapore, and another expanding its operational footprint from Kuala Lumpur. Forest City 2.0 Despite the tailwinds from the SFZ, Li and Syarul acknowledge that transforming the mega project into a self-sustaining regional economy is not without immediate, real-world hurdles. The most pressing challenge currently is cross-border physical connectivity and accessibility. “While the project is geographically proximate to Singapore, seamlessly moving people, goods and daily commuters across borders remains a complex, multi-jurisdictional effort,” says Li. “Furthermore, regional competition from peers like Thailand, Indonesia and Vietnam means that Malaysia must continually sharpen its execution speed and policy delivery to stay ahead.” To close this connectivity gap, Country Garden is taking interim measures while lobbying government authorities for long-term infrastructure approvals. “Before all the major government infrastructure projects are completed, we are bridging the gap ourselves. We currently run daily direct shuttles transferring residents and workers to the Sultan Abu Bakar CIQ Second Link complex,” Li says. For the long term, the developer has submitted plans to the joint Malaysia-Singapore ministerial committee under the Iskandar Regional Development Authority (IRDA) for a dedicated ferry terminal. Once approved, ferry routes will connect Forest City directly to Raffles Marina in Singapore and Batam in Indonesia. “We are also asking the government for assistance to permit a direct highway connection linking straight to Tuas, and to integrate Forest City into upcoming regional rail routes like the RTS [Rapid Transit System], ART [Automated Rapid Transit] and transport corridors heading to Kulai and Senai,” he adds. “Moving people efficiently is crucial to unlocking the full value of the JS-SEZ but because these are country-to-country matters, we have to keep pushing and following up continuously.” Simultaneously, the master developer is pivoting to boosting population density and creating high-value local jobs, away from traditional residential property sales, towards what the team calls “Forest City 2.0”. “We are not launching any more residential projects in the near future, but focusing on clearing the inventory. We will advance commercial and industrial land development earlier than originally scheduled to inject immediate economic vibrancy,” Li says. “Our next focus is to bring in companies and industries to invest or establish their presence here.” Acknowledging the importance of generating sufficient jobs to increase Forest City’s population, CGPV is actively trying to draw data centres, logistics players and manufacturers to its upcoming 418-acre industrial park. “We need to create real economic dynamics. If you don’t generate jobs and economic substance, you cannot sustain a population,” Li stresses. The response to this industrial shift has been positive. In the first half of this year alone, the developer logged over 300 company enquiries and secured a 40-acre industrial land deal with a manufacturer in Phase 1 of the industrial park, paving the way for ready-built factory developments in Phase 2 should market demand sustain. In another strategic partnership, Country Garden recently signed a term sheet with Penang-based Oriental Holdings Bhd (KL:ORIENT) to develop a RM750 million healthcare hub in Forest City, anchored by a 500-bed hospital alongside comprehensive medical supply chain services. “Internationally, we are actively introducing Forest City to big-name [multinational corporations]. It is not so much for their name, but the entire supply chain. We are looking to bring in ‘queen bee’ investors,” Li says. “We have been doing roadshows, especially in China, to introduce the JS-SEZ and Forest City SFZ. We went to Shenzhen and Suzhou, which have some of the most successful industrial parks in China.” Apart from the industrial park, CGPV has also received enquiries from international investors interested in private island parcels. “It is something that we are looking at. Instead of standard residential towers, we can custom-reclaim approved island plots, such as 1.5 to two acres, based entirely on an investor’s specific operational or residential requirements. It’s about being adaptive to what the current market actually demands,” he says. Road to 2030 and beyond Apart from Forest City, Country Garden Malaysia has four other major developments in Johor and the Klang Valley, executed largely through JVs. “Out of our five projects in Malaysia, four are structured as JVs,” Li explains. “Only Danga Bay is 100% held by Country Garden Malaysia. We welcome JVs because local partners bring value to the table, though for master site design, we prefer to lead.” In Johor Bahru, Country Garden Central Park has completed three phases comprising over 3,000 residential units that are nearly fully sold. The developer is now planning subsequent sub-phases over a 10- to 12-year development cycle. In Kuala Lumpur, the initial two phases of township development Lake City in Taman Wahyu are completed and sold out, with Phase 3 scheduled for launch next year. The remaining four parcels have been earmarked for development over a 15-year period. In Semenyih, Selangor, residential development Diamond City launched its final landed parcel in September 2025, which is expected to wrap up construction within two years. With a substantial land bank in its existing portfolio, the developer will focus its resources on executing its active pipeline over the next decade. As the interview draws to a close, both Li and Syarul reflect on the long-term nature of master township development. “Rome was not built in a day,” Li says. “When we first came to this coastal area in Johor, it was completely rural. Today, the infrastructure is firmly established. Development never moves in a straight upward line; it moves in spirals, but it always moves forward. “We wish the public to know that since the first day Country Garden has been here in Malaysia, we have wanted to be here long term. Of course, there are twists and turns over the years, but we cannot deny the contribution of the company in Malaysia.” He says Country Garden has invested RM32 billion in Malaysia, including RM20 billion in Forest City alone. “We have created jobs, contributed to the country’s tax revenues and trained local skilled workers. Most importantly, after so many challenges and uncertainties, we were here, and we are still here today. The fundamentals are in place, and we have absolute faith in what Forest City will become.” Save by subscribing to us for your print and/or digital copy. title: 'Zetrix AI's Business Continuity Uncertain After JPJ Suspension — MBSB Research
body: 'KUALA LUMPUR (Oct 6): Zetrix AI Bhd (KL:ZETRIX) faces uncertainty over its revenue collection business after the Ministry of Transport (MOT) suspended its services as a collection agent for the Road Transport Department (JPJ) over unremitted government funds totalling RM314 million. MBSB Research said that even if Zetrix AI has a proposal to resolve the outstanding remittances, financial liquidity poses an additional hurdle for the group. It noted that Zetrix AI reported cash and cash equivalents of RM541.6 million in the second quarter ended June 30, 2026 (2QFY2026), its short-term loans and borrowings stand higher at RM853.1 million, raising concerns over its ability to make immediate settlement payments. "Thus, we do not discount the possibility that Zetrix AI may have difficulties in making the payment in the near term," said MBSB Research in a note on Tuesday. Even if Zetrix AI manages to clear its arrears, the resumption of its collection agent role is not guaranteed, the research house said. "Potentially, should the group manage to resume the JPJ services, there may be changes in standard operating procedure (SOP) whereby the government revenue would need to be credited immediately. "This would prevent similar incidents from occurring. The group announced that it has submitted a proposal to resolve outstanding remittances and is working towards restoring the affected services, subject to the relevant approvals," it added. Furthermore, MOT’s active promotion of its proprietary MyJPJ application, alongside existing channels such as JPJ counters, kiosks, and the JPJ Public Portal, could diminish the long-term necessity for third-party collection agents. Such operational risks have prompted MBSB Research to place its recommendation and target price on the stock under review. The research house noted that despite four engagement sessions held since May with key stakeholders — including the Ministry of Finance — and 35 reminder notices issued by JPJ, the outstanding arrears remain unsettled. Consequently, MOT and JPJ are preparing to initiate legal proceedings to recover the unremitted funds. Meanwhile, MARC Ratings recently revised its MARCWatch status on Zetrix AI to “negative” from “developing”. MARC cited heightened concerns over corporate governance, transparency, and a lack of material information regarding a sharp rise in borrowings, alongside the recent resignation of the company’s external auditor, TGS TW PLT, due to portfolio rationalisation and resource management. MBSB Research is keeping its earnings forecasts unchanged for now, pending further developments. Non-AI and non-blockchain segments currently account for approximately 40% of the group’s total revenue. title: 'Trading Of MKH Shares To Be Suspended
body: 'Whitmore Holdings Sdn Bhd will proceed with the compulsory acquisition of the remaining shares in MKH Bhd after securing valid acceptances representing at least 90% of the offer shares under its unconditional mandatory takeover offer.  MKH said Bursa Malaysia will suspend trading in its shares upon the expiry of five market days from the extended closing date of the offer.  MKH said it had received a press notice from Maybank Investment Bank Bhd, on behalf of Whitmore and its ultimate offeror Batu Kawan Bhd, confirming that the 90% threshold had been met as at 5pm on Sept 30, 2026.  Whitmore is offering RM2.00 cash per MKH share for all remaining voting shares not already owned by Whitmore and Batu Kawan.  Following the acceptance level, Whitmore and Batu Kawan will invoke subsection 222(1) of the Capital Markets and Services Act 2007 to compulsorily acquire the remaining shares from dissenting shareholders.  A compulsory acquisition notice will be issued to those shareholders within two months from Sept 30.  Following the suspension, Whitmore and Batu Kawan intend to procure MKH to take the necessary steps to withdraw its listing status from Bursa Malaysia’s Official List.  If the delisting is completed, MKH shares will no longer be traded on the Main Market.  The takeover offer will remain open for acceptance until 5pm on Oct 8, 2026.

title: 'EPF Disposes 10 Million Maybank Shares
body: 'The Employees Provident Fund (EPF) has disposed of 10 million shares in Malayan Banking Bhd (Maybank), reducing its direct shareholding in Malaysia’s largest banking group to 12.045%.  Maybank said the disposal took place on Sept 22 through Citigroup Nominees (Tempatan) Sdn Bhd, under an account held for the EPF.  Following the transaction, the retirement fund’s direct interest in Maybank stood at approximately 1.46 billion shares, representing 12.045% of the bank’s issued share capital.  The filing did not disclose the disposal price or total transaction value.  The EPF remains a substantial shareholder in Maybank following the disposal.  Maybank shares closed at 10.22, dropping close to 10% over the last six months.

title: 'AirAsia Indonesia Mulls Share Sales, Liability Restructuring
body: '(Oct 1): PT AirAsia Indonesia is considering restructuring some liabilities and selling shares as the low-cost carrier seeks to repair a balance sheet that has kept its shares suspended since July. The airline is mulling converting trade payables and lease liabilities owed to controlling entities or shareholders into perpetual instruments that would effectively count as equity, according to a Wednesday filing. It is also considering a rights issue or a private placement. The recapitalisation options are unfolding against a much bigger funding squeeze at parent AirAsia Group Bhd (KL:AAGB), which had a record US$4.1 billion (RM16.75 billion) of debt at the end of June and is seeking about US$1 billion in refinancing. Last month, the group’s co-founder and adviser Tan Sri Tony Fernandes said fresh capital would be injected into the Indonesian and Philippine operations, with new shareholders expected to join affiliates. Shares of AirAsia Indonesia have been suspended since early July because its latest financial statements showed negative equity. It has not chosen a path yet and is still assessing funding needs, market conditions and the feasibility of each option with shareholders and outside advisers, it said in the filing. The measures under review are intended to strengthen its capital structure that should also help it comply with exchange requirements, it said.
